newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda calls for measures against coffee disease.
newsitem.headline: Uganda calls for measures against coffee disease.

text.p: A Ugandan minister on Monday appealed to global coffee researchers meeting in Kampala to find ways of fighting and containing a coffee wilt disease devastating the crop in the east African nation.

Kibirige Ssebunya, minister of state for agriculture, told the researchers gathered in the Ugandan capital for a scientific workshop that tracheomycosis disease had hit large parts of the country's coffee-growing areas.
Tracheomycosis destroys a coffee tree's vascular system. It leaves a black sear on the tree stem, after which the tree dies.
"If we do not move quickly we shall no jobs," said Ssebunya, adding that 12 growing districts had been affected by the disease, which was first detected in the country in 1993.
"The biggest problem to Uganda's main cash crop is the disease itself. I looked at devastated villages and felt devastated also," Ssebunya added.
The disease also rampant in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo.
At present, coffee farmers only uproot affected trees once the disease has been located in an area.
Government policy is also to uproot and burn down all affected trees and then keep affected areas free from the crop for two years. It then arranges free seedlings for farmers to replant.
Uganda has also launched a quarantine system restricting movement of robusta coffee across districts.
The disease is widespread in the western districts of Bundibugyo, Kabarole and Rukungiri, where incidence on some smallholder farmers has reached 60-100 percent.
The disease is first reported to have spread to Uganda from the Congo and authorities are worried about it spreading to neighbouring Kenya, Rwanda and Tanzania.
Coffee accounts for 64 percent of Uganda's total foreign exchange earnings.
